```{julia}
#|   10$, $\lambda = 0.05\,\lambda_{\max}$, three random seeds). MM-IRLS tracks
#|   Direct-CD with the gradient strategy as the algebra above predicts---both
#|   stall at the same per-iteration correction fraction. Local-weight IRLS
#|   converges, matching the strategy collapse argument. The Local-IRLS curve
#|   uses Newton at the inner level; the gradient and exact strategies coincide
#|   with it numerically (verified in unit tests).

dd = JLD2.load(@projectroot("results", "sim-irls-comparison.jld2"))
df = DataFrame(dd["results"])
df = flatten(df, [:time, :relgaps, :gaps, :primals])

df.relgaps .= max.(df.relgaps, 1.0e-20)
df.it = "seed = " .* string.(df.it)

spec = data(df) * mapping(:time, :relgaps, color = :strategy, col = :it)

draw(
    visual(Lines) * spec,
    axis = (yscale = log10, ylabel = "Relative duality gap", xlabel = "Time (s)"),
    facet = (; linkxaxes = :none),
    figure = (; size = (800, 250))
)
```

@fig-irls-comparison realizes both predictions empirically: MM-IRLS stalls on
the same plateau as Direct-CD with the gradient strategy under $\mu_0 = 0.99$,
while Local-IRLS converges on the same problem. The strategy-collapse claim
within Local-IRLS is verified numerically in the unit tests rather than the
figure, since by construction the three strategies produce identical iterates on
the inner quadratic.

A reader may notice that Local-IRLS also outpaces Direct-CD with the Newton
strategy on this problem. This reflects the broader trade-off between
algorithmic families rather than a comparison of intercept strategies: IRLS-CD
enjoys a constant inner Hessian and locally quadratic outer convergence, which
favours it on canonical-link GLMs where the linearization is tight. Direct-CD
has the edge when $f'''$ is large (e.g.\
Poisson with extreme rates, where each linearization is loose far from the
current iterate), when working-response instability under saturation matters, or
when screening and working-set methods (standard in modern $\ell_1$ solvers)
compose poorly with re-linearization [@bertrand2022]. Our strategy analysis is
orthogonal to this family choice: within either family, the recommendation
against the gradient strategy and in favour of Newton carries through.

### Geometric Illustration

```{julia}
#| label: fig-parametric
#| fig-cap: Example illustrating the three main intercept fitting strategies
#|   considered in our paper on a simple problem with one feature and an
#|   intercept.
#| fig-show: true
#| message: false

using Intercepts

# Local seed: this figure computes inline (a deterministic illustration that
# doubles as a render-time smoke test of the solver), so seed it independently
# of upstream chunks rather than riding the global RNG state.
Random.seed!(42)

n = 100
p = 1
k = 10
μ0 = 0.9

X, y = generatedata(
    n, p; response = :binomial, μ0 = μ0, x_type = :normal, x_density = 0.9, ρ = 0.99, s = k, amplitude = 1,
)

strategies = [
    (strategy = GradientStrategy(), name = "Gradient"),
    (strategy = NewtonStrategy(), name = "Newton"),
    (strategy = ExactStrategy(), name = "Exact"),
]

reg = 0.2

results = [
    cdsolver(
            X,
            y,
            reg,
            lossfun = LogisticLoss(),
            intercept_strategy = s.strategy,
            save_history = true,
        ) for s in strategies
]

λ = results[1].λ

β0 = range(-0.5, 3.5, length = 100)
β = range(-0.5, 1.2, length = 100)
grid = [(b0, b) for b0 in β0, b in β]

primal_values = zeros(size(grid))

for (i, (b0, b)) in enumerate(grid)
    η = b0 .+ X[:, 1] * b
    primal_values[i] = loss(LogisticLoss(), η, y) + λ * abs(b)
end

fig = Figure()
ax = Axis(
    fig[1, 1],
    xlabel = "Intercept (β₀)",
    ylabel = "Coefficient (β₁)",
)

levels = geomspace(minimum(primal_values), maximum(primal_values), 20)

contour!(β0, β, primal_values, levels = levels, colormap = :grays)

for (res, s) in zip(results, strategies)
    scatterlines!(res.intercepts, dropdims(res.coefs, dims = 1), label = s.name)
end

fig[1, 2] = Legend(fig, ax)

fig
```

## Results {#sec-results}

### Methodology and Reproducibility {#sec-methodology}

All internal-solver experiments use the `Intercepts` Julia package on Julia
1.12 (CI pins 1.12.6, matching the version under which `Manifest.toml` was
generated) with the default OpenBLAS. We report outer-pass counts as the primary work
metric: one pass is one sweep through all $p$ coordinates plus an intercept
update, and "passes to tolerance" use a target relative duality gap of $10^{-8}$
unless noted. Pass budgets (`maxit`) are set generously (1000 for the
single-$\lambda$ figures, 5000 for the heatmap of @sec-imbalance-reg) and are
clipped only at the figure level when the gradient strategy fails to reach the
tolerance; those points appear at the budget cap. All synthetic designs are
standardized (zero mean, unit variance per column) and use cyclic coordinate
ordering unless we explicitly compare orderings; the AR(1) feature correlation
parameter is $\rho = 0.6$ by default. Random seeds are fixed per experiment
script. The heatmap of @sec-imbalance-reg replicates each cell across three
seeds; the other figures use a single seed because cell-to-cell variability is
dwarfed by the strategy effect we are isolating.

Real-data experiments load the LIBSVM problems from a pinned data archive on
Zenodo---the exact inputs behind every real-data figure, retrieved with
`experiments/fetch-data.sh` (see the README)---and the solver standardizes each
column internally before fitting. The production-solver
panel runs glmnet 4.1-10 (R), biglasso 1.6-1 (R), adelie 1.0-8 (R), skglm 0.5
(Python), LIBLINEAR through scikit-learn's `solver="liblinear"` wrapper, and
BlitzL1 at commit `aef8d02` on the shared standardized problem produced by
`experiments/sim-real-problem.jl`. The shared problem is regenerated from
`Random.seed!(2025)`; the production drivers are otherwise deterministic given
the cached `X.csv` / `y.csv`, so each driver runs once per tolerance setting
with no per-driver seed or per-cell replication. Each driver sweeps its native
tolerance knob and writes a CSV under `results/real-solvers/`, which the figures
in @sec-production-solvers read directly. The sweeps cover: glmnet `thresh` and
biglasso `eps` from $10^{-1}$ to $10^{-13}$ in half-decade steps; skglm `tol`
over the same span in quarter-decade steps; LIBLINEAR `tol` from $10^{-1}$ to
$10^{-8}$ and BlitzL1 `tol` from $10^{-1}$ to $10^{-10}$, both in half-decade
steps; adelie's coupled `tol`/`irls_tol` only down to $10^{-3.5}$ because the
outer IRLS convergence criterion exhausts progress long before any iterate cap
at tighter settings. Per-driver iterate caps (glmnet/biglasso `max.iter`
$= 10^{6}$, adelie `irls_max_iters` $= 10^{6}$, skglm `max_iter` $= 5000$,
LIBLINEAR `max_iter` $= 5000$, BlitzL1 `max_iter` $= 500$) are set generously;
operating points that hit the cap appear at the cap.

All experiment outputs are cached. Internal-solver scripts at
`experiments/sim-*.jl` write `.jld2` files to `results/`; production-solver
scripts write `.csv` to `results/real-solvers/`. Figures backed by an experiment
re-render from cache, so to refresh one re-run the corresponding script; the
illustrative @fig-parametric instead runs the solver live at render time, as a
small reproducible example. The Julia, R, and
Python toolchains are pinned by `devenv.nix` (the `glmnet`, `biglasso`,
`adelie`, `skglm`, and `blitzl1` versions above included) and all use their
default OpenBLAS builds with no thread pinning. Hardware: a single x86_64 Linux
workstation with an AMD Ryzen 9 7900 (12 cores, 24 threads) and 64 GB of RAM;
wall-clock numbers in this paper are indicative rather than benchmark-grade. Source code and cached results ship with the paper repository.

### Simulated Data

The first prediction we test in @sec-theory is the Schur-coupling residual
(@eq-grad-residual): the gradient strategy's effective per-pass step on the
intercept is the bare gradient step
shrunk by $H_{00}/L_0$, so the strategy slows as the imbalance $\mu_0$ pushes
$H_{00}$ toward zero with $L_0 = 1/4$ unchanged. @fig-mu-extreme already
exhibits this collapse on the standardized binary-logistic design ($n=500$,
$p=1000$, $s=10$, $\rho = 0.6$, $\lambda = 0.05\,\lambda_{\max}$) used
throughout the simulated experiments below: the gradient strategy is competitive
at $\mu_0 = 0.5$, slows visibly past $\mu_0 = 0.9$, and fails to reach the
tolerance within budget at $\mu_0 = 0.99$, while the Newton and exact strategies
overlay each other across every level. The bare-Newton and exact trajectories
agreeing is the outer-pass content of the within-pass drift
(@eq-intercept-drift); the per-pass inner cost
the two strategies differ on is made visible in @sec-per-pass-cost. The
quantitative scaling of the gradient/Newton ratio with $\mu_0$ and $\lambda$ on
the same design is taken up in @sec-imbalance-reg and @fig-mu-reg-gradient.

### Real Data

The complementary prediction is that the same scaling holds across real problems
with different $(\mu_0,\text{density},n,p)$. We run the three strategies on six
LIBSVM benchmark problems at $\lambda = 0.05\,\lambda_{\max}$, listed in
@tbl-real-logreg-problems and ordered by predicted slowdown
$L_0/H_{00} = 1 / (4 \mu_0 (1 - \mu_0))$ (the table lists its reciprocal
$H_{00}/L_0$). The set spans a $9\times$ range in
$L_0/H_{00}$ and five distinct design families: the Webb web-pages binary w1a, a
subsampled news20.binary bag-of-words text design (news20-3pct, 60 positives and
1\,940 negatives drawn deterministically from `news20.binary`), the UCI Adult
census (a4a) at moderate imbalance, the high-dimensional genomic leukemia
microarray ($n \ll p$, penalty-dominated), the small-$p$ Wisconsin breast cancer
panel, and dense balanced gisette. The two severely-imbalanced points (w1a,
news20-3pct) sit at near-identical $\mu_0$ on very different designs---a
$300$-feature sparse web indicator panel versus a $1.3\,\mathrm{M}$ vocabulary
text bag-of-words---so any framework prediction that survives both is not a
property of the w1a design specifically.

  | dataset       | $n$   | $p$   | density | $\mu_0$ | $H_{00}/L_0$ |
  | :------------ | ----: | ----: | :------ | ------: | -----------: |
  | w1a           | 2,477 |   300 | sparse  |   0.029 |        0.113 |
  | news20-3pct   | 2,000 | 4,675 | sparse  |   0.030 |        0.116 |
  | a4a           | 4,781 |   123 | sparse  |   0.248 |        0.747 |
  | leukemia      |    38 | 7,129 | dense   |   0.711 |        0.823 |
  | breast-cancer |   683 |    10 | dense   |   0.350 |        0.910 |
  | gisette       | 6,000 | 5,000 | dense   |   0.500 |        1.000 |

  : LIBSVM problems used in @fig-real-logreg. $\mu_0$ is the positive-class
    marginal; $H_{00}/L_0 = 4\mu_0(1-\mu_0)$ is the fraction-of-correction
    predicted by @eq-grad-residual. news20-3pct is a 60/1\,940 deterministic
    subsample of `news20.binary`: with `MersenneTwister(42)` seeding a single
    RNG, the positive-class row indices are shuffled and the first 60 retained,
    then the negative-class row indices are shuffled and the first 1\,940
    retained, and the union is sorted to preserve the original row order.
    After subsampling, the $\approx 1.35\,\mathrm{M}$ word features that appear
    in fewer than 20 of the surviving 2\,000 documents are dropped---low-support
    features otherwise standardise to extreme values and destabilise the CD
    solve. {#tbl-real-logreg-problems}

```{julia}
#| label: fig-real-logreg
#| fig-cap: Convergence trajectories for the three intercept strategies on the
#|   six LIBSVM benchmark problems of @tbl-real-logreg-problems at $\lambda =
#|   0.05\,\lambda_{\max}$, ordered left-to-right, top-to-bottom by predicted
#|   slowdown $L_0/H_{00}$. The gradient strategy needs roughly $5\times$ more
#|   passes than Newton on w1a and $\approx 4\times$ more on news20-3pct; the
#|   factor shrinks to $\approx 1.3\times$ on a4a, $\approx 2.3\times$ on
#|   breast-cancer, and the three strategies overlay on leukemia
#|   (penalty-dominated) and gisette (balanced). The exact strategy tracks bare
#|   Newton throughout on every panel, consistent with the per-pass-cost
#|   prediction of @eq-intercept-drift at this tolerance.

dd = JLD2.load(@projectroot("results", "real-logreg.jld2"))
df = DataFrame(dd["results"])
df = flatten(df, [:time, :relgaps, :gaps, :primals])

df.relgaps .= max.(df.relgaps, 1.0e-20)
df.dataset = replace.(
    df.dataset,
    "gisette_scale" => "gisette",
    "news20-imb" => "news20-3pct",
)

dataset_order =
    ["w1a", "news20-3pct", "a4a", "leukemia", "breast-cancer", "gisette"]

spec = data(df) * mapping(
    :time => "Time (s)",
    :relgaps => "Relative duality gap",
    color = :strategy,
    layout = :dataset => sorter(dataset_order...),
)

draw(
    visual(Lines) * spec,
    axis = (yscale = log10,),
    facet = (; linkxaxes = :none),
    figure = (; size = (900, 500))
)
```

@fig-real-logreg confirms the prediction in both directions. The two
severe-imbalance points reproduce the simulated gradient slowdown on very
different sparse designs: w1a ($\mu_0 = 0.029$, a $300$-feature web indicator
panel) needs ${\approx}5\times$ more gradient passes than Newton to relative gap
$10^{-6}$, and news20-3pct ($\mu_0 = 0.030$, a $4\,675$-feature bag-of-words
text panel after dropping low-support vocabulary) reproduces a
${\approx}4\times$ ratio at $10^{-4}$ before hitting the $120\,\mathrm{s}$
wall-time cap. Both sit within the constant-factor offset of the leading-order
$L_0/H_{00}$ prediction that @fig-rate-gap exhibits, and the cross-design
agreement shows the gap is a property of the response imbalance, not of the w1a
design specifically. The mild-slowdown middle (a4a, breast-cancer) gives
gradient/Newton ratios between $1.3$ and $2.3$, consistent with their
$H_{00}/L_0 \in [0.75,\,0.91]$. The two predicted-benign cells are the
framework's negative controls: leukemia ($n \ll p$, penalty-dominated) and
gisette (dense, balanced, $\mu_0 = 0.5$, $H_{00}/L_0 = 1$) both have the three
strategies overlay each other. The exact strategy tracks bare Newton on every
panel, consistent with @eq-intercept-drift at this tolerance.

The Poisson family puts a sharper version of the same prediction on real data.
PoissonLoss has no global upper bound on $f''(\eta) = e^\eta$, so $L_0 = \infty$
and the gradient-strategy update degenerates: the per-pass change is
$-\sum_i (\hat\mu_i - y_i)/(L_0 n) = 0$, an exact no-op on the intercept. We
test this on the congress109 phrase-count corpus of @taddy2015distributed:
$n = 529$ speakers from the 107th--109th US Congress, $p = 999$ political
phrases (the 1\,000-phrase vocabulary with the response phrase removed). The
response $y_i$ is speaker $i$'s count of the phrase `american.people`
($\bar y = 11.83$, $y_{\max} = 396$), the highest-frequency phrase in the
corpus; the features are the remaining $999$ phrase counts after column
standardisation. This is the distributed-multinomial-regression construction
of @taddy2015distributed---a multinomial-over-vocabulary approximated by an
independent Poisson lasso per term---and the baseline rate $\bar y \approx 12$
puts the cold-start intercept overshoot $\bar y - 1 \approx 10.83$ versus the
exact $\log(\bar y) \approx 2.47$ in the regime where the synthetic cold-start
sweep in @fig-cold-start-poisson starts ($\mu_0 = 10$). Same $\lambda =
0.05\,\lambda_{\max}$ convention as the logistic panel; cyclic CD with a
$1\,000$-pass budget.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-real-poisson
#| fig-cap: Convergence trajectories for the four intercept strategies on the
#|   congress109 Poisson problem ($n = 529$, $p = 999$, $\bar y = 11.83$,
#|   $\lambda = 0.05\,\lambda_{\max}$). The gradient strategy is a flat
#|   no-op---$L_0 = \infty$ for PoissonLoss makes the per-pass intercept
#|   update vanish identically, so the iterate cannot benefit from any
#|   imbalance correction and the relative gap plateaus at the cold-start
#|   value (the $\approx 0.31$ asymptote in the figure is the relative gap of
#|   the no-intercept solution). The Newton, unguarded-Newton, and exact
#|   strategies trace a single overlapping curve to relative gap $10^{-10}$
#|   in $\approx 3$ seconds. The per-coordinate Armijo loop inside cdsolver
#|   absorbs the unguarded-Newton transient before the next intercept update
#|   fires, which is why @fig-cold-start-poisson requires $\mu_0 \ge 30$ to
#|   see daylight between the guarded and unguarded curves; congress109 sits
#|   at the lower edge of that regime.

dd = JLD2.load(@projectroot("results", "real-poisson.jld2"))
df = DataFrame(dd["results"])
df = flatten(df, [:time, :relgaps, :gaps, :primals])
df.relgaps .= max.(df.relgaps, 1.0e-20)

spec = data(df) * mapping(
    :time => "Time (s)",
    :relgaps => "Relative duality gap",
    color = :strategy,
)
draw(
    visual(Lines) * spec,
    axis = (yscale = log10,),
    figure = (; size = (600, 380))
)
```

The gradient-strategy collapse in @fig-real-poisson is the strongest empirical
form of the $L_0 = \infty$ structural-inadequacy claim from
@eq-grad-residual---no tuning, no problem-specific imbalance level, just the
loss family. The Newton-class strategies agree on a single trajectory because
the cdsolver's per-coordinate Armijo loop (Tseng--Yun sufficient decrease,
@algo-cd) absorbs the cold-start overshoot before the first intercept update
fires; the synthetic sweep of @fig-cold-start-poisson at $\mu_0 = 10$ shows
the same coincidence and requires $\mu_0 \ge 30$ to separate the guarded and
unguarded curves visibly.

### Cyclic vs Permuted Ordering {#sec-ordering}

The within-pass drift argument of @eq-intercept-drift is agnostic to
coordinate ordering,
but a residual concern is that strict cyclic order deterministically pairs the
intercept solve with the same first coordinate on every pass, which could
compound the drift. Under the per-coordinate Armijo backtrack that the cdsolver
applies after every coordinate update (@sec-methodology), this concern does not
materialise: on the w1a benchmark of @fig-first-example all three strategies
converge under both orderings and the pass-count differences are within a factor
of $1.4$ (@fig-first-example-ordering). Cyclic order is in fact slightly faster
than permuted on this problem for Newton ($157$ vs $187$ passes) and for exact
($149$ vs $197$), with the gradient strategy at $\sim 840$ passes under either
rule. The qualitative ranking of the three strategies---Newton and exact fast,
gradient slow---is the same under both, and we use cyclic CD as the default
elsewhere in the paper.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-first-example-ordering
#| fig-cap: Same configuration as @fig-first-example (w1a, $\lambda =
#|   0.05\,\lambda_{\max}$) under cyclic (top) and permuted (bottom) coordinate
#|   ordering. All three strategies converge to the working tolerance under both
#|   orderings; the choice of ordering rule changes pass counts by at most a
#|   factor of $1.4$ and does not change the qualitative ranking.

dd = JLD2.load(@projectroot("results", "first-example-ordering.jld2"))
df = DataFrame(dd["results"])
df = flatten(df, [:time, :relgaps, :gaps, :primals])

df.relgaps .= max.(df.relgaps, 1.0e-20)

spec = data(df) * mapping(
    :time => "Time (s)",
    :relgaps => "Relative duality gap",
    color = :strategy,
    row = :ordering,
)

draw(
    visual(Lines) * spec,
    axis = (; yscale = log10),
    figure = (; size = (500, 500))
)
```

### Warm-Started Path {#sec-warmstart-path}

The single-$\lambda$ experiments above stress the strategies in their hardest
regime---cold start, large $|\partial_0 F|$ at iterate zero---which is also the
setting in which the theoretical critique of @eq-intercept-drift and the
imbalance collapse of @eq-grad-residual bite hardest. Production users rarely solve a
single $\lambda$ in isolation; they sweep a grid
$\lambda_1 > \lambda_2 > \dots > \lambda_K$ and warm-start each subproblem from
the previous solution. As anticipated in the steelman paragraph above,
warm-starting begins each subproblem with $|\partial_0 F|$ already small. The
Newton-coupling bias (@eq-newton-coupling) then predicts that the bare Newton
step is essentially exact at the start, so $k_0 \in \{1, 2\}$ in the exact strategy and the
$k_0 - 1$ per-pass overhead evaporates. The gradient-strategy collapse should
also soften because the iterate is close to optimum and the $H_{00}/L_0$
shrinkage acts on an already-small residual.

We test this by solving an $\ell_1$-logistic path on two problems---a simulated
standardized design ($n = 500$, $p = 1000$, $s = 10$, $\mu_0 = 0.9$,
$\rho = 0.6$) and the w1a benchmark used in @fig-first-example---over a
geometrically spaced grid of $K = 20$ values from $\lambda_{\max}$ down to
$5 \cdot 10^{-3}\,\lambda_{\max}$. Each subproblem is run to relative-gap
tolerance $10^{-8}$ or to a budget of 300 outer passes / 20 wall-seconds,
whichever comes first. We compare the three strategies, each under both warm
start (initialized from the previous-$\lambda$ solution) and cold start
(re-initialized at zero), and under both cyclic and permuted feature ordering.
The main-text panels show cyclic CD; @fig-warm-start-full and
@fig-warm-start-mechanism-full give the full grid over both orderings.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-warm-start
#| fig-cap: Outer passes per subproblem along a logistic-regression $\lambda$
#|   path (lower is better), under cyclic CD. Solid lines mark warm starts from
#|   the previous $\lambda$; dashed lines mark cold starts at zero. Curves capped
#|   at 300 indicate the pass budget was hit before the tolerance. Left is the
#|   simulated imbalanced problem ($\mu_0 = 0.9$), right is w1a. The
#|   permuted-ordering row is in @fig-warm-start-full.

dd = JLD2.load(@projectroot("results", "sim-warmstart-path.jld2"))
df = DataFrame(dd["results"])
df = flatten(
    df,
    [
        :reg_grid,
        :passes,
        :times,
        :init_relgap,
        :final_relgap,
        :init_partial0F,
        :nnz_solution,
    ],
)

df.start_kind = ifelse.(df.warm_start, "warm", "cold")
df.ordering = ifelse.(df.randomize, "permuted", "cyclic")

# In-text slice: cyclic ordering only (the paper's default; @sec-ordering shows
# permuted differs by ≤1.4× and never changes the ranking). The full
# ordering × dataset grid is @fig-warm-start-full in the appendix.
df_cyclic = filter(:ordering => ==("cyclic"), df)

spec_passes =
    data(df_cyclic) * mapping(
        :reg_grid => "λ / λ_max",
        :passes => "Outer passes",
        color = :strategy,
        linestyle = :start_kind => "Start",
        col = :dataset,
    )

draw(
    visual(Lines) * spec_passes,
    axis = (xscale = log10, yscale = log10),
    figure = (; size = (800, 320)),
)
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-warm-start-mechanism
#| fig-cap: Magnitude of the intercept partial derivative $|\partial_0 F|$ at
#|   the initial iterate of each subproblem along the same $\lambda$ path, under
#|   cyclic CD. Cold start (dashed) is independent of $\lambda$---the initial
#|   iterate is always zero, so $|\partial_0 F|$ is the marginal class imbalance
#|   and the three strategies coincide on top of each other. Warm start (solid)
#|   shrinks $|\partial_0 F|$ by several orders of magnitude, placing each
#|   subproblem in the regime where @eq-newton-coupling predicts strategy
#|   differences to compress. The permuted-ordering row is in
#|   @fig-warm-start-mechanism-full.

spec_partial =
    data(df_cyclic) * mapping(
        :reg_grid => "λ / λ_max",
        :init_partial0F => "|∂₀F| at initialization",
        color = :strategy,
        linestyle = :start_kind => "Start",
        col = :dataset,
    )

draw(
    visual(Lines) * spec_partial,
    axis = (xscale = log10, yscale = log10),
    figure = (; size = (800, 320)),
)
```

The mechanism panel (@fig-warm-start-mechanism) verifies the premise:
warm-starting drives $|\partial_0 F|$ toward zero as $\lambda$ shrinks and the
previous-$\lambda$ solution moves closer to the current optimum. Cold start, by
contrast, sets the initial iterate to zero at every $\lambda$, so
$|\partial_0 F|$ is the marginal class imbalance---roughly $10^2$ on the
simulated problem and $1.2 \times 10^3$ on w1a, identical across strategies.

The pass-count panel (@fig-warm-start) shows the predicted compression with one
caveat. On both problems and both orderings, warm-starting trims the few
pass-budget-capped subproblems for the Newton and exact strategies (on w1a
from $2$--$4$ out of $20$ cold to $2$ out of $20$ warm, depending on ordering
and strategy) and brings their curves on top of each other---this is the
steelman prediction of @eq-intercept-drift: with $|\partial_0 F|$ already small,
the
$k_0 - 1$ per-pass penalty of the exact strategy evaporates. Warm-starting also
tightens the bare Newton solve at very small $\lambda$ on w1a, where the
cold-start trajectory hits the pass budget at relative gaps two to three orders
of magnitude looser than its warm-start counterpart.

The compression is uneven, however. The gradient strategy is essentially
unaffected by warm-starting on w1a---both cold and warm hit the pass budget on
$11$--$12$ of $20$ subproblems, with the curves overlaying. This is
@eq-grad-residual biting at every subproblem: the imbalance factor
$H_{00}/L_0$ remains microscopic at the warm-start iterate, so even a
near-optimal starting point cannot compensate for the shrinking correction. The
simulated problem ($\mu_0 = 0.9$) sits in the milder regime where all three
strategies are competitive cold, and warm-start contributes only a uniform
$\sim 5\%$ reduction in pass count across the board.

The takeaway: warm-starting validates the steelman for Newton-class strategies
(bare Newton and the exact strategy converge to each other) but does not extend
the gradient strategy's scope. The recommendation that follows from
@eq-intercept-drift---bare Newton in direct CD, exact strategy at the
prox-Newton/IRLS boundary---stands,
with the addendum that the exact strategy becomes a defensible alternative
to bare Newton whenever a path solve is in fact used.

### Per-Pass Cost Decomposition {#sec-per-pass-cost}

The pass-count and wall-clock figures above conflate two distinct quantities
that the within-pass drift (@eq-intercept-drift) separates: the *number of
outer passes* needed to reach a tolerance and the *per-pass inner cost* paid
at the intercept update. The claim there is that the exact strategy pays
$k_0 - 1$ extra inner Newton
steps per outer pass with no commensurate rate improvement, where
$k_0 = O(\log\log(1/\varepsilon))$ is the number of inner steps consumed to
drive $|\partial_0 F| < \varepsilon$ at the end of the pass via quadratic Newton
convergence on the 1D intercept subproblem. We instrument the solver to record
$k_0$ for every outer pass and compare the resulting cost trajectories against
the relative-gap trajectories on the imbalanced simulated design of
@fig-mu-extreme ($n = 500$, $p = 1000$, $s = 10$, cyclic CD,
$\lambda / \lambda_{\max} = 0.05$, tolerance $10^{-8}$), sweeping
$\mu_0 \in \{0.5,\,0.9,\,0.99\}$ to vary the cold-start magnitude of
$|\partial_0 F|$.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-per-pass-cost
#| fig-cap: Per-pass inner Newton steps $k_0$ consumed at the intercept update
#|   by the exact strategy, as a function of outer-pass index, across three
#|   imbalance levels. The dashed reference at $k_0 = 1$ marks the Newton
#|   strategy, which takes exactly one inner step by construction. The exact
#|   strategy's $k_0$ spikes at cold start ($k_0 = 6$ on the most imbalanced
#|   design) and tapers to one as the iterate approaches the joint optimum. The
#|   area above the reference is the cumulative wasted inner work predicted by
#|   the within-pass drift (@eq-intercept-drift).

dd = JLD2.load(@projectroot("results", "sim-per-pass-cost.jld2"))
df = DataFrame(dd["results"])
df = flatten(df, [:pass, :inner_steps, :cum_inner_steps, :relgap_after, :time])
df.μ0_label = "μ₀ = " .* string.(df.μ0)
df_exact = filter(:strategy => ==("exact"), df)

spec_cost =
    data(df_exact) * mapping(
        :pass => "Outer pass",
        :inner_steps => "Inner Newton steps per pass (k₀)",
        col = :μ0_label,
    ) * visual(Lines)

spec_ref = mapping([1]) * visual(HLines, linestyle = :dash, color = :gray)

draw(
    spec_cost + spec_ref,
    facet = (; linkyaxes = :all),
    figure = (; size = (800, 260)),
)
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-per-pass-progress
#| fig-cap: Relative duality gap after each outer pass on the same runs. The two
#|   strategies trace nearly indistinguishable trajectories despite the exact
#|   strategy paying 19--62 % more inner Newton steps in total (compare
#|   cumulative areas in @fig-per-pass-cost). The extra inner work per pass
#|   therefore buys no measurable per-pass rate improvement, the empirical
#|   content of the "cost-without-rate-improvement" reading of
#|   @eq-intercept-drift.

spec_prog =
    data(df) * mapping(
        :pass => "Outer pass",
        :relgap_after => "Relative duality gap",
        color = :strategy,
        col = :μ0_label,
    )

draw(
    visual(Lines) * spec_prog,
    axis = (yscale = log10,),
    facet = (; linkyaxes = :all),
    figure = (; size = (800, 260)),
)
```

The two figures together make the $k_0 - 1$ overhead claim concrete.
@fig-per-pass-cost shows $k_0$ peaking at the cold-start pass (6, 4, and 3 inner
steps for $\mu_0 = 0.99,\,0.9,\,0.5$ respectively) and decaying to one by the
time the iterate is near the joint optimum. The relative overhead summed across
the run---total inner Newton steps for the exact strategy divided by the Newton
strategy's pass-count baseline---is $1.30\times$ at $\mu_0 = 0.5$, $1.50\times$
at $\mu_0 = 0.9$, and $1.59\times$ at $\mu\_0 =
0.99$, scaling monotonically with the imbalance that drives $|\partial_0 F|$ at
cold start. @fig-per-pass-progress shows that this extra inner work does not
translate into faster per-pass progress: both strategies trace essentially the
same relative-gap curve and finish in comparable pass counts (Newton:
109/107/121; exact: 109/108/120). The wasted-work claim is therefore
quantitatively visible: the gap between the two curves in @fig-per-pass-cost
integrates to strictly positive inner Newton work for which
@fig-per-pass-progress records no return.

The penalty here is modest because quadratic Newton convergence on the 1D
intercept subproblem keeps $k_0 = O(\log\log(1/\varepsilon))$, well below the
inner-loop cap of 20, and most passes need only a single inner step. The regime
where @eq-intercept-drift bites hardest is the cold-start, large-$|\partial_0 F|$
window of the first few outer passes; the steelman regimes in
@sec-warmstart-path are precisely those where this window is avoided.

### Imbalance and Regularization {#sec-imbalance-reg}

The single-$\lambda$ experiments above test the framework along one axis at a
time. The quantitative prediction of @prp-rate-gap is two-dimensional: the
gradient/Newton pass-count ratio scales with $L_0/H_{00}(\hat\eta)$, and both
$\lambda$ and $\mu_0$ shift $\hat\eta$ and therefore $H_{00}$. We sweep
$\mu_0 \in \{0.5, 0.7, 0.9, 0.95, 0.99\}$ against
$\lambda/\lambda_{\max} \in \{0.5, 0.2, 0.1, 0.05, 0.02, 0.01\}$ on the
standardized binary-logistic design of @fig-mu-extreme (3 seeds per cell),
running each strategy to a relative-gap tolerance of $10^{-8}$ or a budget of
5000 outer passes. We report pass counts rather than wall-clock to decouple the
per-coordinate Lipschitz-mismatch prediction from BLAS and memory effects.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-mu-reg-gradient
#| fig-cap: Pass-count ratio $T_{\mathrm{gradient}} / T_{\mathrm{Newton}}$
#|   (log~10~ scale) across the $(\mu_0,\,\lambda/\lambda_{\max})$ plane,
#|   averaged over three seeds. Cells where the gradient strategy hits the
#|   5000-pass budget are clipped; the ratio there is a lower bound. Ratio
#|   increases monotonically with $\mu_0$ along every column and with
#|   $1/\lambda$ along every row, matching the qualitative form of
#|   @prp-rate-gap.

dd = JLD2.load(@projectroot("results", "sim-mu-reg-heatmap.jld2"))
df = DataFrame(dd["results"])

agg = combine(
    groupby(df, [:μ0, :reg, :strategy]),
    :passes => mean => :passes,
)

wide = unstack(agg, [:μ0, :reg], :strategy, :passes)
wide.gradient_ratio = wide.gradient ./ wide.newton
wide.exact_ratio = wide.exact ./ wide.newton
wide.reg_str = string.(wide.reg)
wide.μ0_str = string.(wide.μ0)

spec_grad =
    data(wide) * mapping(
        :reg_str => sorter("0.5", "0.2", "0.1", "0.05", "0.02", "0.01") => "λ / λ_max",
        :μ0_str => sorter("0.5", "0.7", "0.9", "0.95", "0.99") => "μ₀",
        :gradient_ratio => log10 => "log₁₀(T_grad / T_Newton)",
    )

draw(
    spec_grad * visual(Heatmap),
    figure = (; size = (560, 320)),
)
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-mu-reg-exact
#| fig-cap: Pass-count ratio $T_{\mathrm{exact}} / T_{\mathrm{Newton}}$ (log~10~
#|   scale) on the same grid as @fig-mu-reg-gradient, on a centered diverging
#|   colormap with $|\log_{10} \mathrm{ratio}| \le 0.1$. The heatmap is flat at
#|   zero (white) across the plane---outer-pass-equivalent exact vs Newton, the
#|   prediction of @eq-intercept-drift.

spec_exact =
    data(wide) * mapping(
        :reg_str => sorter("0.5", "0.2", "0.1", "0.05", "0.02", "0.01") => "λ / λ_max",
        :μ0_str => sorter("0.5", "0.7", "0.9", "0.95", "0.99") => "μ₀",
        :exact_ratio => log10 => "log₁₀(T_exact / T_Newton), range ±0.1",
    )

draw(
    spec_exact * visual(Heatmap),
    scales(Color = (; colormap = :RdBu, colorrange = (-0.1, 0.1))),
    figure = (; size = (560, 320)),
)
```

@fig-mu-reg-gradient is monotone in $\mu_0$ across every column: at fixed
$\lambda$, increasing imbalance grows the gradient/Newton pass-count ratio from
roughly one at $\mu_0 = 0.5$ to about ten at $\mu_0 = 0.99$,
$\lambda = 0.01\,\lambda_{\max}$, where the gradient strategy saturates the
5000-pass budget (the ratio there is a lower bound). At
$\lambda = 0.05\,\lambda_{\max}$ (the working regime along glmnet's path) the
empirical ratios across the five $\mu_0$ values are
$\{1.0, 1.1, 1.8, 3.0, 6.8\}$, against an iterate-level
$L_0/H_{00}(\hat\eta) = \{3.2, 3.3, 4.4, 5.7, 12.3\}$ measured at the
Newton-converged iterate on the same cells (mean over three seeds). The
prediction sits a constant factor above empirical that narrows from
$\sim 3\times$ at $\mu_0 = 0.5$ to $\sim 2\times$ at $\mu_0 = 0.99$. The cold-start
proxy $L_0/H_{00}(0) = 1/(4\mu_0(1-\mu_0)) = \{1.00, 1.19, 2.78, 5.26, 25.25\}$
is looser still at high imbalance because active features pull $H_{00}$ above
its intercept-only value $\mu_0(1-\mu_0)$ at this $\lambda$. As $\lambda$
shrinks the active set widens, $H_{00}$ falls toward and beyond
$\mu_0(1-\mu_0)$, and the empirical ratio grows: at
$\lambda = 0.01\,\lambda_{\max}$ the empirical row for
$\mu_0 \in \{0.5, 0.7, 0.9, 0.95\}$ is $\{1.7, 1.8, 4.0, 5.4\}$; the
$\mu_0 = 0.99$ corner is omitted because both Newton and gradient saturate the
5000-pass budget there and the ratio collapses to a meaningless
$\approx 2\times$.

@fig-mu-reg-exact is flat at zero (ratio $\approx 1$) across the plane, with no
cell departing from the unit ratio by more than about 12 %. This is the
outer-pass content of @eq-intercept-drift: the exact strategy consumes the same
number of outer passes as bare Newton when both converge. The cost of the exact
strategy is therefore an inner-step overhead, not an outer-pass overhead---the
quantitative form of which is the $k_0 - 1$ wasted-inner-work claim of
@sec-per-pass-cost. Together the two heatmaps verify @prp-rate-gap on a 30-cell
grid: the gradient strategy carries a Lipschitz-mismatch penalty whose
pass-count signature scales with $\mu_0$ and $1/\lambda$, and the convergence
strategy does not.

This grid, with @fig-rate-gap and @fig-rho-centering, fixes the level at which
@prp-rate-gap holds: scaling and monotonicity, not magnitude. The empirical
ratio reproduces every trend the proposition predicts---it diverges as the
intercept channel degrades ($H_{00}/L_0 \to 0$) and grows monotonically with
$\mu_0$, with $1/\lambda$, and with the design coupling $\bar\rho^2$. The
magnitude is another matter: across this grid the empirical ratio runs a roughly
constant factor of two to four below the iterate-level @eq-rate-gap prediction
(@fig-mu-reg-gradient), the expected signature of @eq-rate-gap being a ratio of
upper bounds built from heuristic substitutions rather than the
iteration-complexity ratio itself. The same constant-factor offset appears in
the single-$\lambda$ sweeps: the iterate-level curve sits above the empirical
ratio in @fig-rate-gap, and the leading-order centering ratio of
@fig-rho-centering, a first-order approximation rather than the full bound, sits
a comparable factor below it. The divergence curves are therefore predictions of
shape, not tight point predictions of $T_{\mathrm{G}}/T_{\mathrm{N}}$.

### Production Solvers {#sec-production-solvers}

The strategy-class predictions of the previous sections are tested here against
six production solvers---across both predicted directions---on three imbalanced
logistic problems: the synthetic design of @fig-irls-comparison ($n = 500$,
$p = 1000$, $s = 10$, nominal $\mu_0 = 0.99$, realized positive-class fraction
$0.878$), w1a from LIBSVM ($n = 2477$, $p = 300$, $\mu_0 = 0.029$, sparse binary
features), and news20-3pct, a $3\%$-positive subsample of LIBSVM news20.binary
documented in @tbl-real-logreg-problems ($n = 2000$, $p = 4\,675$,
$\mu_0 = 0.030$, sparse text features). The three problems together span both
directions of imbalance ($\mu_0$ near 0 and near 1) and three regimes ($p > n$
dense Gaussian, $n > p$ sparse binary, $n < p$ sparse text). Each problem fixes
$\lambda = 0.05 \cdot \lambda_{\max}$. All solvers are run in their recommended
path mode (warm-start from $\lambda_{\max}$ down to $\lambda$ in 50 geometric
steps);[^cold-start-footnote] for each solver we sweep its convergence tolerance
and record the actual work performed (number of CD passes, outer iterations, or
wall-clock time, depending on what the solver exposes) and the primal objective
at termination. Suboptimality is plotted against work, both on a logarithmic
scale. The reference primal $F^\star$ is taken as the minimum primal achieved by
that solver across all configurations on each problem.

[^cold-start-footnote]: At single $\lambda$ without warm-starting, biglasso
    `alg.logistic = "Newton"` and adelie exhibit the unguarded-Newton cold-start
    failure of @eq-newton-coupling on the two extreme-imbalance real datasets
    used here; @sec-cold-start-diag reports the diagnostic.

We sort these solvers into two buckets by the intercept update each realizes on
the original loss (@tbl-classification). Bucket A, the gradient strategy, holds
the MM-IRLS and constant-Lipschitz solvers---glmnet `modified.Newton`, biglasso
`MM`, and skglm---each taking one $L_0 = 1/4$ step per outer iteration. Bucket B,
the Newton strategy, holds the local-IRLS solvers---glmnet `Newton`, biglasso
`Newton`, and adelie---each driving the intercept to its conditional optimum on
every quadratic surrogate. The framework predicts Bucket A to stall under
imbalance and Bucket B to converge fast; the two prox-Newton solvers (LIBLINEAR,
BlitzL1) reach the exact strategy at each subproblem boundary and sit outside the
A/B split.

The within-package mode comparisons (glmnet, biglasso) isolate the weight-scheme
choice: identical solver, identical problem, identical tolerance, only the IRLS
weighting changes. The third panel runs skglm 0.5, the cleanest production
realization of constant-Lipschitz proximal CD at the time of writing, where the
intercept update is the gradient strategy with $L_0 = 1/4$ by construction (a
step $4/n$ against the unaveraged-loss gradient skglm computes internally). The
within-skglm controlled experiment that follows it (@fig-skglm-controlled)
sharpens this further into a same-solver same-problem comparison across the two
skglm commits that bracket the intercept-update fix, on the same $(\mu\_0,
\lambda)$ grid as @fig-mu-reg-gradient. The fourth panel verifies the
complementary prediction on LIBLINEAR (newGLMNET) and BlitzL1, two prox-Newton
solvers whose intercept reaches its conditional optimum at each prox-Newton
boundary (BlitzL1 via an explicit post-step Newton loop on the original loss,
LIBLINEAR via the inner CD's handling of the unregularized intercept) and that
the framework predicts should converge fast. A fifth panel runs adelie
[@yang2024], a recent local-IRLS solver that places the intercept implicitly at
the optimum of each Gaussian surrogate through a weighted-centered-features
parameterization. The framework places adelie in the same bucket as glmnet
`Newton` and biglasso `Newton`, and predicts fast convergence in the working
tolerance regime.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-real-glmnet
#| fig-cap: glmnet `type.logistic = "Newton"` (Bucket B, local-IRLS) versus
#|   `"modified.Newton"` (Bucket A, MM-IRLS with $w \equiv 1/4$) across three
#|   problems---left, the shared synthetic imbalanced logistic problem ($n=500$,
#|   $p=1000$, $\mu_0 = 0.99$); middle, w1a, a real severely imbalanced LIBSVM
#|   problem ($n=2477$, $p=300$, $2.9\%$ positive class); right, news20-3pct, a
#|   $3\%$-positive subsample of LIBSVM news20.binary ($n=2000$, $p=4\,675$
#|   after the $\ge 20$-nonzero column filter documented in
#|   @tbl-real-logreg-problems). All panels use glmnet's recommended path mode
#|   (warm-start from $\lambda_{\max}$ down to $0.05\,\lambda_{\max}$ in $50$
#|   geometric steps); the work axis is total inner CD passes to reach the final
#|   $\lambda$. The within-package gap is a property of the intercept update,
#|   not of any single problem regime ($p > n$ dense Gaussian, $n > p$ sparse
#|   binary, and $n < p$ sparse text).

df = vcat(
    DataFrame(CSV.File(@projectroot("results", "real-solvers", "glmnet.csv"))),
    DataFrame(CSV.File(@projectroot("results", "real-solvers", "w1a", "glmnet.csv"))),
    DataFrame(
        CSV.File(@projectroot("results", "real-solvers", "news20-3pct", "glmnet.csv")),
    ),
)
df = transform(
    groupby(df, :problem),
    :primal => (p -> max.(p .- minimum(p), 1.0e-15)) => :subopt,
)
df.mode = df.type

spec =
    data(df) * mapping(
        :npasses,
        :subopt,
        color = :mode,
        layout = :problem => sorter("synthetic", "w1a", "news20-3pct"),
    )
draw(
    visual(Lines) * spec + visual(Scatter) * spec,
    axis = (
        xscale = log10,
        yscale = log10,
        xlabel = "Inner CD passes",
        ylabel = "Primal suboptimality",
    ),
    figure = (; size = (1000, 300)),
)
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-real-biglasso
#| fig-cap: biglasso `alg.logistic = "Newton"` (Bucket B, local-IRLS) versus
#|   `"MM"` (Bucket A, MM-IRLS) across the same three problems as
#|   @fig-real-glmnet. The within-package gap is an independent confirmation of
#|   the glmnet result on a different codebase. biglasso documents its MM option
#|   as the memory-efficient choice for out-of-core data; the analysis here
#|   quantifies its convergence cost.

df = vcat(
    DataFrame(CSV.File(@projectroot("results", "real-solvers", "biglasso.csv"))),
    DataFrame(
        CSV.File(@projectroot("results", "real-solvers", "w1a", "biglasso.csv")),
    ),
    DataFrame(
        CSV.File(@projectroot("results", "real-solvers", "news20-3pct", "biglasso.csv")),
    ),
)
df = transform(
    groupby(df, :problem),
    :primal => (p -> max.(p .- minimum(p), 1.0e-15)) => :subopt,
)
df.mode = df.alg

spec =
    data(df) * mapping(
        :npasses,
        :subopt,
        color = :mode,
        layout = :problem => sorter("synthetic", "w1a", "news20-3pct"),
    )
draw(
    visual(Lines) * spec + visual(Scatter) * spec,
    axis = (
        xscale = log10,
        yscale = log10,
        xlabel = "Inner CD passes",
        ylabel = "Primal suboptimality",
    ),
    figure = (; size = (1000, 300)),
)
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-real-skglm
#| fig-cap: skglm 0.5 `AndersonCD` across the same three problems as
#|   @fig-real-glmnet. The solver uses constant per-coordinate Lipschitz steps
#|   with the global $1/4$ majorant for the logistic Hessian and updates the
#|   intercept with step $4/n$ against the unaveraged-loss gradient, equivalent
#|   to the gradient strategy with $L_0 = 1/4$ on the averaged loss of
#|   @sec-theory. The trajectory on the synthetic panel exhibits a slow early
#|   ramp (hundreds of outer iterations spent reducing suboptimality before
#|   sharp convergence once the intercept has caught up); this is the
#|   @eq-grad-residual signature, matching the rate-gap prediction of
#|   @prp-rate-gap on a production gradient-strategy solver. The
#|   post-convergence scatter at high
#|   $n_{\text{iter}}$ reflects Anderson acceleration's non-monotonic stopping
#|   behaviour near $F^\star$.

df = vcat(
    DataFrame(CSV.File(@projectroot("results", "real-solvers", "skglm.csv"))),
    DataFrame(CSV.File(@projectroot("results", "real-solvers", "w1a", "skglm.csv"))),
    DataFrame(
        CSV.File(@projectroot("results", "real-solvers", "news20-3pct", "skglm.csv")),
    ),
)
df = transform(
    groupby(df, :problem),
    :primal => (p -> max.(p .- minimum(p), 1.0e-15)) => :subopt,
)
df = df[df.n_iter .> 0, :]
sort!(df, [:problem, :n_iter])

spec =
    data(df) * mapping(
        :n_iter,
        :subopt,
        layout = :problem => sorter("synthetic", "w1a", "news20-3pct"),
    )
draw(
    visual(Lines) * spec + visual(Scatter) * spec,
    axis = (
        xscale = log10,
        yscale = log10,
        xlabel = "AndersonCD outer iterations",
        ylabel = "Primal suboptimality",
    ),
    figure = (; size = (1000, 300)),
)
```

Across the three solvers the prediction holds: within-package weight toggles in
glmnet and biglasso produce the predicted slowdown of the constant-majorant
mode, and skglm 0.5---the only production solver in our survey whose intercept
update is unambiguously the gradient strategy---exhibits the slow-ramp signature
that the Newton-coupling bias (@eq-newton-coupling) and the Schur-coupling
residual (@eq-grad-residual) together predict. The same
diagnosis motivated a pull request to skglm replacing the gradient update with a
Newton step; the change was merged upstream as commit `8f9cbd77`.[^skglm-pr]

[^skglm-pr]: <https://github.com/scikit-learn-contrib/skglm/pull/337>, merged
    2026-05-13. skglm 0.6 is unreleased at the time of writing; the controlled
    comparison below pins the two relevant commits directly.

@fig-real-glmnet through @fig-real-skglm each compare the two within-package
modes across three problems: the shared synthetic imbalanced design ($n=500$,
$p=1000$, $\mu_0 = 0.99$, dense Gaussian), w1a (real, $n > p$, sparse binary,
$\mu_0 = 0.029$), and news20-3pct (real, $n < p$, sparse text, $\mu_0 = 0.030$);
each problem fixes $\lambda = 0.05\,\lambda_{\max}$. The three regimes together
test whether the within-package gap is a property of the intercept update or of
any single problem construction. All these trajectory panels---glmnet,
biglasso, and skglm here, and the @fig-real-proxnewton and @fig-real-adelie
panels that follow---fix one $(\mu_0, \lambda)$ per problem, so they establish
the *direction* of the strategy-class split (Bucket A slow, Bucket B fast)
rather than how the Bucket-A slowdown scales across the $(\mu_0,\,\lambda)$
plane. That sweep is the work of two 30-cell grids on the same plane: the
in-house @fig-mu-reg-gradient and its production-solver companion
@fig-skglm-controlled below. Cross-package comparisons remain confounded by
between-package algorithmic differences. The merged skglm patch eliminates that
confound on the skglm row. With `b03644fe` (the last commit before the fix,
behaviourally identical to the released 0.5) and `8f9cbd77` (the merge
introducing the Newton intercept update) we can run the same `AndersonCD` driver
against itself, on the same problem-generation pipeline, and isolate the
intercept-update change. @fig-skglm-controlled reports the pass-count ratio
between the two commits across the 30-cell $(\mu_0,\,\lambda/\lambda_{\max})$
grid. The empirical pattern matches the in-house heatmap: the ratio sits near
unity at low imbalance and grows monotonically with $\mu_0$ and $1/\lambda$,
with no other algorithmic differences confounding the comparison.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-skglm-controlled
#| fig-cap: Within-skglm controlled comparison. Pass-count ratio
#|   $T_{\mathtt{b03644fe}} / T_{\mathtt{8f9cbd77}}$ (log~10~ scale) of skglm's
#|   `AndersonCD` solver before and after the intercept-update fix introduced by
#|   the merged pull request, averaged over three seeds, across the same
#|   $(\mu_0,\,\lambda/\lambda_{\max})$ grid as @fig-mu-reg-gradient. Cells
#|   where the pre-fix commit hits the 5000-iteration cap are clipped; the ratio
#|   there is a lower bound. The monotone increase in $\mu_0$ and $1/\lambda$
#|   matches the prediction of @prp-rate-gap on a production solver whose only
#|   change between the two trials is the intercept update.

df_sk = DataFrame(
    CSV.File(@projectroot("results", "skglm-controlled", "results.csv")),
)
df_sk.strategy = ifelse.(df_sk.commit .== "b03644fe", "gradient", "newton")

agg_sk = combine(
    groupby(df_sk, [:mu0, :reg, :strategy]),
    :n_iter => mean => :n_iter,
)
wide_sk = unstack(agg_sk, [:mu0, :reg], :strategy, :n_iter)
wide_sk.skglm_ratio = wide_sk.gradient ./ wide_sk.newton
wide_sk.reg_str = string.(wide_sk.reg)
wide_sk.μ0_str = string.(wide_sk.mu0)

spec_sk =
    data(wide_sk) * mapping(
        :reg_str => sorter("0.5", "0.2", "0.1", "0.05", "0.02", "0.01") => "λ / λ_max",
        :μ0_str => sorter("0.5", "0.7", "0.9", "0.95", "0.99") => "μ₀",
        :skglm_ratio => log10 => "log₁₀(T_pre / T_post)",
    )

draw(
    spec_sk * visual(Heatmap),
    figure = (; size = (560, 320)),
)
```

The fourth panel verifies the complementary prediction: solvers whose intercept
update is the exact strategy at a prox-Newton boundary should converge fast.
LIBLINEAR (newGLMNET) and BlitzL1 are the two production solvers in our survey
that fit this description. @fig-real-proxnewton reports their wall-clock cost to
reach $F^\star$ across the same three problems used above, complementary to the
inner-pass curves for skglm 0.5 (which uses the gradient strategy on the
intercept) and glmnet's `modified.Newton` (the constant-majorant alternative).

```{julia}
#| label: fig-real-proxnewton
#| fig-cap: LIBLINEAR (newGLMNET) and BlitzL1 across the same three problems as
#|   @fig-real-glmnet. Both are prox-Newton solvers whose intercept reaches its
#|   conditional optimum at each prox-Newton boundary (BlitzL1 via an explicit
#|   post-step 1-D Newton loop on the original loss, LIBLINEAR via the inner
#|   CD's handling of the unregularized intercept), the complement of
#|   `glmnet::Newton` and `biglasso::Newton` from @fig-real-glmnet and
#|   @fig-real-biglasso. The wall-clock cost to reach $F^\star$ is the evidence
#|   that exact-strategy behaviour on the intercept does not inherit the
#|   imbalance failure mode of the gradient-strategy solvers. LIBLINEAR runs
#|   that hit its internal `max_iter` cap without further progress have been
#|   excluded---they reflect a tolerance-semantic quirk in the library, not
#|   useful work-quality data. Wall-clock time is used as the work axis because
#|   the two solvers count outer iterations differently and BlitzL1 does not
#|   expose an iteration counter on its solution object.

df = vcat(
    DataFrame(CSV.File(@projectroot("results", "real-solvers", "proxnewton.csv"))),
    DataFrame(
        CSV.File(@projectroot("results", "real-solvers", "w1a", "proxnewton.csv")),
    ),
    DataFrame(
        CSV.File(
            @projectroot("results", "real-solvers", "news20-3pct", "proxnewton.csv"),
        ),
    ),
)
df = transform(
    groupby(df, :problem),
    :primal => (p -> max.(p .- minimum(p), 1.0e-15)) => :subopt,
)
df = df[.!(df.solver .== "LIBLINEAR" .&& df.n_iter .>= 5000), :]
sort!(df, [:problem, :solver, :runtime])

spec =
    data(df) * mapping(
        :runtime,
        :subopt,
        color = :solver,
        layout = :problem => sorter("synthetic", "w1a", "news20-3pct"),
    )
draw(
    visual(Lines) * spec + visual(Scatter) * spec,
    axis = (
        xscale = log10,
        yscale = log10,
        xlabel = "Time (s)",
        ylabel = "Primal suboptimality",
    ),
    figure = (; size = (1000, 300)),
)
```

The fifth panel adds an independent codebase confirmation for the
convergence-on-the-local-quadratic bucket. adelie\ [@yang2024] is a recent
direct-Newton solver that builds the same weighted Gaussian surrogate as glmnet
`Newton` but realizes the intercept implicitly: rather than updating $\beta_0$
as a coordinate inside the inner CD pass, it weighted-centers the features at
the start of each surrogate and tracks the residual mean, reconstructing
$\beta_0 = \bar{y} + \overline{\mathrm{resid}}$ at the end of the inner solve.
The intercept therefore sits at the surrogate's optimum on every outer pass by
construction, with no separate update step. The classification places adelie in
the same bucket as glmnet `Newton` and biglasso `Newton`, and @fig-real-adelie
reports its per-tolerance wall-clock cost across the same three problems used
above. adelie's outer-IRLS criterion is coarser than glmnet's coefficient-based
`thresh`, which is reflected in a higher achievable suboptimality from a single
tolerance sweep; the per-iteration cost---the prediction at stake here---is on
the same order as the other local-IRLS solvers.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-real-adelie
#| fig-cap: adelie [@yang2024] across the same three problems as
#|   @fig-real-glmnet. The solver is a local-IRLS implementation that keeps the
#|   intercept implicit through a weighted-centered-features parameterization of
#|   the Gaussian surrogate, so on each surrogate the intercept is at the
#|   optimum by construction. The framework places it in the same bucket as
#|   glmnet `Newton` and biglasso `Newton`. The per-tolerance wall-clock cost in
#|   the working tolerance regime is the evidence for the exact-strategy
#|   prediction. Tighter tolerances are bounded by adelie's outer-IRLS criterion
#|   $|\sum (\mathrm{resid} - \mathrm{resid}_{\mathrm{prev}}) \cdot (\eta -
#|   \eta_{\mathrm{prev}})| \le \texttt{irls\_tol}$, which has trouble making
#|   progress under imbalance and effectively places a floor on the achievable
#|   suboptimality from a single tolerance sweep---a property of the criterion,
#|   not of the per-iteration cost.

df = vcat(
    DataFrame(CSV.File(@projectroot("results", "real-solvers", "adelie.csv"))),
    DataFrame(CSV.File(@projectroot("results", "real-solvers", "w1a", "adelie.csv"))),
    DataFrame(
        CSV.File(@projectroot("results", "real-solvers", "news20-3pct", "adelie.csv")),
    ),
)
df_ref = vcat(
    DataFrame(CSV.File(@projectroot("results", "real-solvers", "skglm.csv"))),
    DataFrame(CSV.File(@projectroot("results", "real-solvers", "w1a", "skglm.csv"))),
    DataFrame(
        CSV.File(@projectroot("results", "real-solvers", "news20-3pct", "skglm.csv")),
    ),
)
F_star = combine(groupby(df_ref, :problem), :primal => minimum => :F_star)
df = leftjoin(df, F_star, on = :problem)
df.subopt = max.(df.primal .- df.F_star, 1.0e-15)
sort!(df, [:problem, :tol])

spec =
    data(df) * mapping(
        :tol,
        :subopt,
        layout = :problem => sorter("synthetic", "w1a", "news20-3pct"),
    )
draw(
    visual(Lines) * spec + visual(Scatter) * spec,
    axis = (
        xscale = log10,
        xreversed = true,
        yscale = log10,
        xlabel = "Convergence tolerance (tol = irls_tol)",
        ylabel = "Primal suboptimality",
    ),
    figure = (; size = (1000, 300)),
)
```

#### Poisson Family

The Poisson family separates the production solvers structurally before any
trajectory is recorded. PoissonLoss has $f''(\eta) = e^\eta$ unbounded on
$\mathbb{R}$, so no global Lipschitz upper bound exists; consequently neither
the $w \equiv 1/4$ MM majorant of glmnet `modified.Newton` and biglasso `MM`
nor the constant-Lipschitz coordinate step of skglm `AndersonCD` has a
Poisson analog. The status of each solver on this family is structural, not
empirical:

- **glmnet** supports `family = "poisson"` with a single fitting mode
  (local-IRLS); no `type.poisson` switch exists.
- **biglasso** does not implement `family = "poisson"` at all; its signature
  is restricted to `gaussian`, `binomial`, `cox`, and `mgaussian`.
- **skglm** `AndersonCD` requires `datafit.get_lipschitz()`, which the
  `Poisson` datafit declines to implement (`AttributeError: Poisson is not
  compatible with solver AndersonCD`). The Bucket-A entry vanishes at the
  attribute-resolution layer.
- **skglm** `ProxNewton` pairs with the `Poisson` datafit through local
  prox-Newton subproblems and is the prox-Newton representative in the
  panel.
- **adelie** supports `glm.poisson(y)` through the same direct-Newton /
  weighted-centered-features parameterisation as the logistic case.

Three Bucket-B solvers therefore remain: glmnet, adelie, and skglm
`ProxNewton`. We run each in path mode on congress109 with $\lambda =
0.05\,\lambda_{\max}$, sweeping the solver-specific tolerance.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-real-poisson-production
#| fig-cap: Three Bucket-B production solvers on the congress109 Poisson
#|   problem ($n = 529$, $p = 999$, $\bar y = 11.83$, $\lambda =
#|   0.05\,\lambda_{\max}$), each in path mode (warm-start from
#|   $\lambda_{\max}$ down to $\lambda$ in $50$ geometric steps). Primal
#|   suboptimality (vertical) versus wall-clock time (horizontal); reference
#|   $F^\star$ taken as the minimum primal observed across all three solvers
#|   and tolerances. The three trajectories agree on $F^\star$ to within
#|   $\approx 10^{-5}$ and converge in well under a second; glmnet reaches
#|   the tightest reported suboptimality, adelie's outer-IRLS criterion
#|   places a floor at $\approx 10^{-4}$ as in @fig-real-adelie, and skglm
#|   `ProxNewton` plateaus after $\approx 15$ outer prox-Newton iterations.
#|   The Bucket-A panel is absent by construction (skglm `AndersonCD` and
#|   biglasso are structurally unavailable for Poisson, see above) and there
#|   is no within-package mode toggle the way @fig-real-glmnet shows for
#|   logistic; every working solver on Poisson is local-IRLS-equivalent.

probdir = @projectroot("results", "real-solvers-poisson", "congress109")
df_gl = DataFrame(CSV.File(joinpath(probdir, "glmnet.csv")))
df_ad = DataFrame(CSV.File(joinpath(probdir, "adelie.csv")))
df_pn = DataFrame(CSV.File(joinpath(probdir, "proxnewton.csv")))

df = vcat(
    DataFrame(solver = "glmnet", runtime = df_gl.runtime, primal = df_gl.primal),
    DataFrame(solver = "adelie", runtime = df_ad.runtime, primal = df_ad.primal),
    DataFrame(solver = "skglm ProxNewton", runtime = df_pn.runtime, primal = df_pn.primal),
)
F_star = minimum(df.primal)
df.subopt = max.(df.primal .- F_star, 1.0e-15)
sort!(df, [:solver, :runtime])

spec = data(df) * mapping(
    :runtime,
    :subopt,
    color = :solver,
)
draw(
    visual(Lines) * spec + visual(Scatter) * spec,
    axis = (
        xscale = log10,
        yscale = log10,
        xlabel = "Time (s)",
        ylabel = "Primal suboptimality",
    ),
    figure = (; size = (700, 380)),
)
```

The Poisson panel therefore makes a structural rather than an empirical
point: the within-package weight-scheme toggle that drives @fig-real-glmnet
and @fig-real-biglasso has no analog here, not because the production
authors chose to omit it but because the underlying loss family does not
admit the $w \equiv 1/4$ surrogate that powers the Bucket-A entries. Every
working Poisson solver in production CD lives in Bucket B---a closed-form
read of the framework's recommendation, expressed at the source-code level
rather than the trajectory level.

#### Single-Lambda Cold Start {#sec-cold-start-diag}

The path-mode protocol used above warm-starts the inner CD past the cold-start
transient at $\beta = 0$. At single $\lambda$ without that ramp, the
unguarded-Newton intercept update predicted to be unstable by
@eq-newton-coupling fails in production code on the two extreme-imbalance real
problems. The diagnostic in @tbl-cold-start-diag runs each solver at
$\lambda = 0.05\,\lambda_{\max}$ with $\text{eps} = 10^{-1}$, sweeping the
iterate cap from $10^1$ to $10^5$; reference primal $0.0497$ from path mode on
both datasets.

  | dataset     | solver                             | $\beta_0$                      | primal  | iterations             |
  | :---------- | :--------------------------------- | :----------------------------- | ------: | :--------------------- |
  | w1a         | biglasso `alg.logistic = "Newton"` | $-723$ (range $[-1722, -291]$) | $16.19$ | $10^5$ cap, oscillates |
  | w1a         | biglasso `alg.logistic = "MM"`     | $-3.51$                        | $0.088$ | $2$                    |
  | w1a         | adelie                             | ---                            |     --- | empty state returned   |
  | news20-3pct | biglasso `alg.logistic = "Newton"` | $-3.48$                        | $0.310$ | $2$ (premature stop)   |
  | news20-3pct | biglasso `alg.logistic = "MM"`     | $-3.48$                        | $0.089$ | $2$                    |
  | news20-3pct | adelie                             | $-5.22$                        | $0.052$ | converges              |

  : Single-lambda cold-start outcomes. biglasso `Newton` diverges on w1a
    ($\beta_0$ oscillates over four orders of magnitude across the iterate-cap
    sweep with primal stuck near $10^1$) and exits its eps criterion prematurely
    on news20-3pct (primal $\approx 6\times$ the path-mode optimum). adelie
    returns an empty solution state on w1a regardless of `irls_max_iters`, which
    is its surface form of the same cold-start failure. biglasso `MM` (the $w
    \equiv 1/4$ global majorant, Bucket A) converges in two iterations on both
    problems. Diagnostic script: `experiments/sim-cold-start-real.R`; full
    sweep: `results/real-solvers/cold-start-diag.csv`. {#tbl-cold-start-diag}

The intercept-specific reading of @tbl-cold-start-diag is that the global
majorant $L_0 = 1/4$ is an $X$-free safeguard---two scalars ($n$ and $\bar y$)
determine the step---and absorbs the cold-start transient at trivial cost on the
unpenalized coordinate, where the corresponding fix for a coefficient coordinate
would require column-norm information. The unguarded-Newton mode is the default
in biglasso and the only mode in adelie, so on a benchmark like w1a a user who
omits path mode receives no solution. The dataset-dependence at matched $\bar y$
(catastrophic on w1a, mild on news20-3pct) reflects that the failure is
triggered by the IRLS weight collapse after the first inner solve rather than by
the cold-start gradient magnitude alone; the working-quadratic on news20-3pct's
wider sparse design pulls many entries to zero under the $\ell_1$ penalty before
the linear predictor reaches extreme values, dampening the cycle.

## Discussion

The picture that emerges across theory and experiments is that the intercept
update is not a one-line implementation detail but a load-bearing choice whose
right setting is dictated by the response distribution. For direct coordinate
descent on a smooth GLM loss, the recommendation is the Newton block step with
an Armijo backtracking safeguard: it is locally invariant to imbalance,
requires no tuning, and matches the exact strategy on outer-pass count while
avoiding the $k_0 - 1$ wasted inner work that the exact strategy spends per
pass. The one scoped exception is the warm-started path setting of
@sec-warmstart-path: with $|\partial_0 F|$ already small at each warm-started
subproblem, the $k_0 - 1$ per-pass penalty of the exact strategy evaporates
and it becomes a defensible alternative whenever a path solve is in fact used.

The Armijo guard belongs in the recommendation unconditionally rather than as
a conditional add-on the user must select by loss family. On bounded-Hessian
losses (logistic, quadratic) it is invisible: @fig-cold-start shows the bare
and guarded variants produce indistinguishable trajectories at every $\mu_0$
level we tested, including the adversarial cold start at $\mu_0 = 0.99$,
because the guard never fires. On unbounded-Hessian losses such as Poisson at
extreme rates (@fig-cold-start-poisson) the same guard becomes load-bearing:
bare Newton overshoots the cold-start intercept by a factor that scales with
$\mu_0$, and although the cdsolver's per-coordinate backtracking absorbs the
transient eventually, the guarded variant descends monotonically while the
unguarded variant exhibits a pass-one relative gap several orders of magnitude
above. The gradient strategy, by contrast, fails outright on real Poisson data
(congress109, @fig-real-poisson): $L_0 = \infty$ makes the per-pass intercept
update vanish identically and the iterate plateaus at the cold-start relative
gap, while the Newton-class strategies agree on a single trajectory. The same
Lipschitz mismatch $H_{00}/L_0$ that shrinks toward zero under imbalance
produces the order-of-magnitude pass-count gaps in @fig-mu-extreme,
@fig-mu-reg-gradient, and the gradient curve of @fig-multinomial-sweep.

The structural classification of production solvers in @sec-production-solvers
tightens the recommendation into a diagnostic: given a CD-based GLM solver, the
intercept-update strategy it realises predicts whether its inner solve will slow
under imbalance, independent of the rest of the algorithm. The classification
places glmnet `Newton`, biglasso `Newton`, adelie, LIBLINEAR, and BlitzL1 in the
safe bucket and glmnet `modified.Newton`, biglasso `MM`, and skglm 0.5 in the
imbalance-sensitive bucket, with the predicted pass-count separation confirmed
empirically on three imbalanced problems (@fig-real-glmnet--@fig-real-adelie).
The within-package mode toggles in glmnet and biglasso turn this into a
controlled experiment whose outcome is consistent with the framework. The
Poisson family carries the same diagnostic one step further:
@fig-real-poisson-production shows the Bucket-A entry vanishing at the
attribute layer rather than the trajectory layer (skglm `AndersonCD` rejects
the Poisson datafit because `get_lipschitz` is unimplemented; biglasso
ships no Poisson family at all), so every working production Poisson CD
solver is local-IRLS-equivalent by construction. This is the framework's
prediction read directly from the source code.

The multinomial setting amplifies the practical relevance of the choice. Whereas
binary logistic regression needs an explicit imbalance ($\mu_0$ near zero or
one) to expose the gradient-strategy stall, the $(K-1)$-block intercept Hessian
distributes the same failure mode across every rare class, so any classification
problem with a long-tailed label distribution sits in the regime where the
gradient strategy is slow on at least one intercept coordinate
(@fig-multinomial-imbalance, @fig-multinomial-sweep). The same multinomial block
structure couples the Newton step with the exact strategy, so the residual
scalar wedge collapses---a structural property rather than a tuning artefact, as
the 2-D sweep shows.

Two limitations bound the present analysis. First, the Newton-strategy results
are *local*: @eq-newton-error and @eq-newton-coupling are Taylor identities
for a single Newton step, not a global convergence proof for
CD-with-Newton-intercept, and the empirical evidence in @sec-results stands in
for that. A tighter rate analysis under restricted strong convexity would let
@prp-rate-gap predict the empirical pass-count constant rather than only its
scaling and monotonicity (@sec-imbalance-reg). Second, the production-solver
experiments in @sec-production-solvers run on a single shared problem; the
heatmap of
@sec-imbalance-reg replicates the binary direct-CD predictions across a 30-cell
grid but the cross-package comparison does not yet sweep the $(\mu_0, \lambda)$
plane. Extending the production-solver sweep along those axes, and verifying the
multinomial predictions against glmnet's symmetric-multinomial path and adelie's
multi-response solver, are natural follow-ups.

# Supplementary Figures {.unnumbered}

These are the full versions of the dense grids that the main text shows as
representative slices: the complete multinomial sweep
(@fig-multinomial-sweep-full, sliced to its four corners in
@fig-multinomial-sweep) and the warm-started-path grids over both coordinate
orderings (@fig-warm-start-full and @fig-warm-start-mechanism-full, shown for
cyclic CD only in @fig-warm-start and @fig-warm-start-mechanism).

```{julia}
#| label: fig-multinomial-sweep-full
#| fig-cap: Full version of @fig-multinomial-sweep, the complete $4 \times 4$
#|   sweep over the rarest-class marginal $\bar p_K \in \{0.05, 0.02, 0.01,
#|   0.005\}$ (rows, top to bottom) and feature amplitude $\in \{0.5, 1.0, 1.5,
#|   2.0\}$ (columns, left to right). The Newton and exact strategies overlap on
#|   a single curve in every one of the sixteen cells; the gradient strategy
#|   stalls progressively harder as $\bar p_K$ shrinks and as amplitude grows.

dd = JLD2.load(@projectroot("results", "sim-multinomial-imbalance-sweep.jld2"))
df = DataFrame(dd["results"])
df = flatten(df, [:time, :relgaps, :gaps, :primals, :pass])

df.relgaps .= max.(df.relgaps, 1.0e-20)

agg = combine(
    groupby(df, [:p_K, :amplitude, :strategy, :pass]),
    :relgaps => median => :relgaps,
)

agg.p_K_str = "p̄_K = " .* string.(agg.p_K)
agg.amp_str = "amp = " .* string.(agg.amplitude)

spec = data(agg) * mapping(
    :pass => "Pass",
    :relgaps => "Relative primal suboptimality",
    color = :strategy,
    row = :p_K_str => sorter("p̄_K = 0.05", "p̄_K = 0.02", "p̄_K = 0.01", "p̄_K = 0.005"),
    col = :amp_str => sorter("amp = 0.5", "amp = 1.0", "amp = 1.5", "amp = 2.0"),
)

draw(
    visual(Lines) * spec,
    axis = (yscale = log10,),
    facet = (; linkxaxes = :none),
    figure = (; size = (800, 600)),
)
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-warm-start-full
#| fig-cap: Full version of @fig-warm-start. Outer passes per subproblem along
#|   the logistic-regression $\lambda$ path, with cyclic CD (top row) and
#|   permuted CD (bottom row); left column the simulated imbalanced problem
#|   ($\mu_0 = 0.9$), right column w1a. Solid lines mark warm starts, dashed
#|   lines cold starts; curves capped at 300 hit the pass budget before the
#|   tolerance.

dd = JLD2.load(@projectroot("results", "sim-warmstart-path.jld2"))
df = DataFrame(dd["results"])
df = flatten(
    df,
    [
        :reg_grid,

        :times,
        :init_relgap,
        :final_relgap,
        :init_partial0F,

)

df.ordering = ifelse.(df.randomize, "permuted", "cyclic")

    data(df) * mapping(
        :reg_grid => "λ / λ_max",

        row = :ordering,

draw(
    visual(Lines) * spec_passes,
    axis = (xscale = log10, yscale = log10),
    figure = (; size = (800, 500)),
)
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-warm-start-mechanism-full
#| fig-cap: Full version of @fig-warm-start-mechanism. The intercept partial
```
